title: Balanced Literacy, Structured Literacy, and the Problem with Labels
author: Michelle Ruhe
summary: K-5 literacy coach Michelle Ruhe argues that misunderstanding of labels drives much of the reading wars. She opens with a colleague who said she never learned phonics because she was taught with balanced literacy, when what she described was look-say or whole-word instruction, which is not balanced literacy at all. Ruhe defines balanced literacy as balancing all components of effective instruction, including explicit phonics, comprehension, reading, writing, speaking and listening, with authentic chances to apply skills. Her remedy is to pause and ask clarifying questions before debating, and to name what each person means by strong literacy instruction, whether balanced, structured or comprehensive. She then lists common ground: systematic phonics matters, literacy is more than phonics, background knowledge and vocabulary are crucial, and explicit instruction is powerful. She concludes that no framework is a silver bullet and that educators should move past label-driven shutdowns toward the shared aim of skilled, confident readers and writers.
points: A teacher's claim that she was taught with balanced literacy actually described whole-word memorization, showing how loosely the label is used.
Ruhe's definition of balanced literacy includes explicit phonics alongside comprehension, writing, speaking and listening, so phonics-free instruction cannot be balanced.
The first step in any literacy debate is to ask what the other person means by the label and what they remember of it.
Educators already agree on more than the debate suggests: systematic phonics, background knowledge, vocabulary and explicit instruction all matter.
Neither balanced nor structured literacy is a silver bullet, and the terms now trigger shutdown before listening begins.
quotes: I immediately stopped her. I reminded her that if phonics wasn’t taught, it was absolutely not balanced literacy. That’s not balanced at all.

It means balancing all the components of effective literacy instruction, including explicit phonics, comprehension, reading, writing, speaking, and listening. And it means students get authentic, meaningful opportunities to apply skills.
Before we ever enter into a conversation, especially one that may lead to a misunderstanding, let’s just pause for a beat.

We have to also name what we say is strong literacy instruction. Whether that means balanced or structured or comprehensive literacy. Whatever you name it, it’s important to define what it looks like to you.

Most teachers I know recognize that systematic phonics instruction matters. We might differ in our approach, the amount of time we devote to it, and the degree to which we integrate it into the instructional day.
No single framework or approach is a silver bullet. Silver bullets don’t exist.

Right now, we’re at a point where just hearing the words “structured literacy” or “balanced literacy” causes a complete shutdown. Hearing one of these terms, all too often, puts up an impenetrable wall.
Because at the end of the day, this isn't about defending a label. And it’s not about winning an argument.
